lines.text: New Windsor. Decr 28th 1780.
D Sir;
I have the pleasure of introdu
cing to your acquaintance the Marquis de la
Fayette a Majr Genl. and as an officr of rank in those of France, in the American Army, his
family, fortune & illustrious connexions in
France are alone sufficient to entitle him to our
highest respect, but when the obligation which
America is under to him for his
early attachment to her rights – his great Zeal
& powerful support of her cause are known
I am persuaded it will give you pleasure
to show him every civility in your power.
It is probable that he may be accom
panied by his Brother in law the Count de
Noailles, & Count de Damas, two Gentn. of fami
ly, fortune & rank in the French Army at
Rhode Island, whose Zeal to serve as marins leads them to make
a Southern Campaign this winter, if they
can obtain permission of the Count de Rochambeau
Commanding the French Army at Rhode Island
– Should this event take place I beg leave
to recommend them also to your attention.
With much esteem & regard
I am D Sir
Yr. Most obedt. Servt
G Washington

modernization.modern_text: New Windsor. Decr [?] 28th 1780. Dear Sir; I have the pleasure of introducing to your acquaintance the Marquis de la Fayette a Major General and as an officer of rank in those of France, in the American Army, his family, fortune & illustrious connexions in France are alone sufficient to entitle him to our highest respect, but when the obligation which America is under to him for his early attachment to her rights – his great Zeal & powerful support of her cause are known I am persuaded it will give you pleasure to show him every civility in your power. It is probable that he may be accompanied by his Brother in law the Count de Noailles, & Count de Damas, two Gentlemen of family, fortune & rank in the French Army at Rhode Island, whose Zeal to serve as marines [?] leads them to make a Southern Campaign this winter, if they can obtain permission of the Count de Rochambeau Commanding the French Army at Rhode Island – Should this event take place I beg leave to recommend them also to your attention. With much esteem & regard I am Dear Sir Your Most obedient Servant George Washington
modernization.plain_english: Dear Sir, I am pleased to introduce the Marquis de la Fayette to you. He is a major general in the American army and an officer of high rank in France. His family, wealth, and famous connections in France deserve our highest respect. Furthermore, America owes him a great debt for his early support of our rights, his great enthusiasm, and his powerful backing of our cause, so I am sure you will be glad to show him every possible courtesy. He might be joined by his brother-in-law, the Count de Noailles, and the Count de Damas. They are well-born, wealthy, and high-ranking gentlemen in the French army at Rhode Island, and their eagerness to serve as marines leads them to join a southern campaign this winter, provided they get permission from Count de Rochambeau, who commands the French army in Rhode Island. If this happens, I ask that you also look out for them. With much esteem and regard, I am your most obedient servant, George Washington.
modernization.summary: George Washington writes a letter of introduction for the Marquis de la Fayette, a major general in the American army, asking the recipient to treat him with great respect and civility. Washington also recommends two other French noblemen, the Count de Noailles and the Count de Damas, if they participate in a southern campaign during the winter.

annotations.context: Written in late December 1780 from New Windsor, George Washington introduces the Marquis de Lafayette and several other French officers to an unnamed recipient. At this stage in the American Revolutionary War, the alliance with France was crucial, and French forces under Rochambeau were stationed in Rhode Island, coordinating potential movements with Washington's army.
annotations.why_it_matters: This letter highlights the international diplomacy and personal relationships that sustained the Franco-American alliance, which was indispensable to achieving American independence.
discussion_questions: How does Washington leverage both Lafayette's personal status and his military contributions to encourage the recipient to welcome him?
What does the mention of the Count de Noailles and Count de Damas seeking a southern campaign reveal about the mobility and coordination of French forces in America?
Why would letters of introduction like this one be vital for military leaders and diplomats during the 18th century?
